title: Business Impact Analysis
summary: A business impact analysis is the analytical step that identifies an organisation's critical business processes, the resources they depend on, and the consequences of each process stopping for a given length of time. Its output sets the recovery objectives that later drive resilience spending: the recovery time objective states how long a process may be unavailable, and the recovery point objective states how much data loss measured in time is tolerable, which together decide where investment goes first. It is not a risk assessment, because it describes impact and dependency rather than the likelihood of a threat, and it is not a list of systems, because the analysis is organised around business services and only then traced down to the applications, data, people, and suppliers that support them. The work depends on interviews with the people who actually run each process, since only they know the manual workarounds and hidden dependencies that documents omit. The common mistake is to run the exercise from an information technology asset list or to let leadership guess the outage tolerance, which produces recovery targets that are either unrealistically strict or dangerously relaxed.

exercises.title: Business Impact Analysis - EASY
exercises.summary: Recall and recognition: definitions, one clear answer, single-step questions.

exercises.title: Business Impact Analysis - MEDIUM
exercises.summary: Application: read a short log or alert and choose the correct next step.

exercises.title: Business Impact Analysis - HARD
exercises.summary: Analysis: a multi-step scenario with distractors, evidence to weigh, and a reason to give.

exercises.title: Business Impact Analysis - EXTREMELY HARD
exercises.summary: Synthesis under pressure: incomplete evidence, competing priorities, and a decision you must defend.

beginner.definition: A business impact analysis finds out which parts of a company matter most and what happens if they stop. It records how long each part can be offline before real harm begins. It also shows how much data the company can afford to lose. The results decide what the company protects and repairs first.
beginner.whyItMatters: Not every system is equally important, and treating them all the same wastes money. If you never measure the harm of a stop, you cannot choose sensible recovery targets. You may spend a lot on a system that can wait for days. Meanwhile a small system that blocks all deliveries stays unprotected. Measurement turns guesses into clear priorities.
howItWorks: You list the services the company sells and the processes that deliver them.
You interview the people who run each process and ask what it depends on.
You describe what happens when each process stops for one hour, one day, or one week.
You agree the longest acceptable stop and the most acceptable data loss for each one.
You trace each process down to the systems, suppliers, people, and data it needs.
You rank the processes and use that order to plan recovery and spending.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital at night. If the computer system for patient records stops, staff can manage on paper for about an hour. After four hours, planned operations are delayed. After a full day, patients must be sent to another hospital. Each stage has a different cost and risk. The night staff tell you these limits, because they see them every week.
takeaways: Ask the people who run the process, not only the managers above them.
Set recovery targets from measured impact, then buy protection to match them.
Review the analysis when services, suppliers, or systems change.

objectives: Explain what a business impact analysis is and why an organisation performs one.
Describe how impact is measured across time for a single business process.
Explain the meaning of recovery time objective and recovery point objective.
Distinguish a business impact analysis from a risk assessment and from asset inventory work.
Describe how dependencies on suppliers and people are identified during analysis.
Explain how the results drive priorities in continuity and recovery planning.
